I gather you were starting Rserve from R using Rserve()? In that case your R session that you use to start Rserve has absolutely nothing to do with Rserve - it simply starts the Rserve program (as it shows on the command line). If you wanted to temporarily serve the contents of your interactive R session, you'd have to use run.Rserve() insead (but that is mostly used for debugging only). So, yes, using either the eval/source directives in the configuration or the --RS-source command line flags is the way you would deploy static code in Rserve. You can obviously also source during the client request -- this is useful for prototyping as you don't need to restart the server.

Are you sure that you are not using a personal R library?  Its not a
good idea to put your packages in the \Program Files tree. From a
fresh R session enter this:

.libPaths()

and if there are two components then your personal R library is the
first.  Your personal library is likely at
%userprofile%\Documents\R\win-library\2.15
and R_LIBS should be set to it.

I would try this first:

set R_HOME=C:\PROGRA~1\R\R-215~1.2
jgr-1_62.exe --rhome=%R_HOME%

and if that works you are done. If not (and it does not work on my
system) then try this if its true that you have a personal R library
at the location I have assumed above (or some variation if your
personal library is elsewhere):

set R_HOME=C:\PROGRA~1\R\R-215~1.2
set R_LIBS=%userprofile%\Documents\R\win-library\2.15
set R_LIBS_USER=%R_LIBS%;%R_HOME%\library
jgr-1_62.exe --rhome=%R_HOME% --libpath=%R_LIBS%

If you really have no personal library (i.e. .libPaths() gives a
single component and that component is in \Program Files) then try
this if the above are no good:

set R_HOME=C:\PROGRA~1\R\R-215~1.2
set R_LIBS=%R_HOME%\library
set R_LIBS_USER=%R_LIBS%
jgr-1_62.exe --rhome=%R_HOME% --libpath=%R_LIBS%

Also for modularity try to re-use environment variables set in earlier
set statements in your later statements for consistency.  You would
have never had a spaces problem had that been done.

Java doesn't support explicit unloading. The only way to unload a class is if *all* its object instances *and* the class loader get garbage-collected by Java. rJava already uses custom loader which you have access to so you could daisy-chain another instance of the rJava loader that you keep under your control, but I'm still not sure how you can make Java to garbage-collect it at the point you need it ...

Dear readers,

At this moment I am trying to build a web-service around the GeMTC R
package. The GeMTC R package depends on rJava to call some functionality in
Java, which it needs to function.

I am wondering how this might work out on a (Linux) Rserve environment.
Currently I'm importing the library once during startup by passing library
to eval in the Rserve.conf. But does this mean that for each new
RConnection a new JVM will be spun up, or that the new connections try
(possibly concurrently) to call the one JVM through rJava?

Thanks in advance!

Joel Kuiper

> Dear readers,

> At this moment I am trying to build a web-service around the GeMTC R package. The GeMTC R package depends on rJava to call some functionality in Java, which it needs to function.
> 
> I am wondering how this might work out on a (Linux) Rserve environment. Currently I'm importing the library once during startup by passing library to eval in the Rserve.conf. But does this mean that for each new RConnection a new JVM will be spun up, or that the new connections try (possibly concurrently) to call the one JVM through rJava? 
> 

What you put in the eval statement of the configuration file is executed once in the server instance. So there is only one JVM instance, but as the new connections connect it will get forked. As I said in the previous e-mail this is typically not supported by JVMs. The only safe way is to start the JVM only after the client has connected.

Cheers,
Simon
